summaries.summary: Cyberbullying is defined by the National Crime Prevention Council, affects between to 10% to 40% of internet users, and can cause effects from temporary anxiety to suicide.
Cyberbullying detection is challenging because definitions, topics, vocabulary, platform-specific semantics, communication styles, evolving words, hashtags, and anonymity vary across SMPs.
Past cyberbullying detection works have Bottleneck B1, Bottleneck B2, and Bottleneck B3, while this work targets Formspring, Twitter, and Wikipedia for personal attack, racism, and sexism.
The authors experimented with logistic regression, support vector machine, random forest, naive Bayes, CNN, LSTM, BLSTM, BLSTM with Attention, and several word representation methods.
Experiments use large, diverse, manually annotated, publicly available datasets from Formspring, Twitter, and Wikipedia talk pages, with class imbalance and truncation at the 95 percentile post size.
Formspring was a question and answer based website whose dataset includes 12K annotated question and answer pairs, with 825 labeled as containing cyberbullying content.
The Twitter dataset includes 16K annotated tweets, with 3117 labeled as sexist, 1937 as racist, and the remaining marked as neither sexist nor racist.
The Wikipedia dataset includes over 100k labeled discussion comments from English Wikipedia's talk pages, with 13590 comments labeled as personal attack.

Preliminary analysis shows swear word usage and anonymity are unreliable for cyberbullying detection, with 78% of Formspring swearing posts non-bullying and 82% of Twitter bullying posts using no swear words.

Cyberbullying detection has been recognized since 2003, addressed automatically since 2009, and typically uses single SMP datasets, handcrafted features, traditional machine learning, F1 score, and accuracy.
The authors experimented with CNN, LSTM, BLSTM, and BLSTM with attention, which differ only in the Neural Architecture layer and use increasing neural complexity and information.
The embedding layer processes fixed size word sequences using random, GloVe, or SSWE initialization, with dimension size 50 and no significant variation from 30 to 200.
Models use dropout rates of 0.25 and 0.5, a fully connected layer, softmax, backpropagation, Adam, categorical cross-entropy, and learn task-specific word embeddings.
Traditional machine learning models LR, SVM, RF, and NB with character n-gram and word unigram representations performed significantly lower than DNN models.
All DNN models were implemented using Keras, with preprocessing, five-fold cross-validation, and performance reported for each trained model.
Oversampling bullying posts thrice improved all DNN models, especially Formspring with 825 bullying instances, and replication rate of three was good enough.

Initial word embeddings do not significantly affect cyberbullying detection with oversampling, while without oversampling the CNN and BLSTM with attention performance gap reduces as dataset size increases.
Table TABREF20 compares four DNN models using SSWE, showing LSTM usually performs weaker and the other three models have no significant performance gap.
Learned embeddings from BLSTM with attention show topic-specific clusters after t-SNE dimensionality reduction, with words relevant to each bullying topic forming clusters.
Word meanings change across cyberbullying topics, as Twitter considers slave similar to targets of racism and sexism while Wikipedia does not show such bias.
Transfer learning was used with BLSTM with attention to test whether knowledge from one dataset improves cyberbullying detection on other datasets.
Complete Transfer Learning (TL1) gave significantly low recall, relatively higher precision, and showed Formspring and Wikipedia cyberbullying nature is more similar than Twitter.
Feature Level Transfer Learning (TL2) dramatically improved recall and significantly improved precision, indicating learned word embeddings are essential for knowledge transfer across datasets.
Model Level Transfer Learning (TL3) did not significantly improve over TL2, indicating network weights are not essential and learned word embeddings are key knowledge.
DNN models with transfer learning beat best-known results, achieving F1 scores of 0.94 for Wikipedia and Twitter and F1 score of 0.95 with accuracy score of 98% for Formspring.
DNN models with transfer learning beat state of the art results for all three datasets and may improve with profile, social graph, and severity information.
